documents.abstract: Introduction In Norway, the early education and care (ECEC) sector has the highest rate of work-related fatigue and sickness absence across all sectors. Work in ECEC can be characterized as physically and emotionally demanding, which may lead to fatigue and the two most common causes of sickness absence in the ECEC sector, i.e., musculoskeletal and mental health issues. Improvements to the work environment can lead to better health for ECEC employees and improve ECEC quality. Therefore, work environment, employee health, and ECEC quality go Hand-in-Hand. This paper presents the protocol for conducting a trial to evaluate the effectiveness and implementation of the tailored participatory Hand-in-Hand workplace intervention. Methods and analysis The study is a 1-year pragmatic cluster-randomized controlled trial with a wait-listed control group. Nineteen ECEC centers were recruited from two Norwegian municipalities, with an estimated 350 employees. The intervention is facilitated by external consultants and includes one workshop and two workplace visits. This includes training the employees in the Hand-in-Hand toolbox, a systematic method for developing workplace measures. Data collection will consist of accelerometer and heart rate measurements, questionnaires, diaries, interviews and registry data; baseline measurements were conducted in October/November 2025. The primary outcome of the effect evaluation will be work-related fatigue. The effectiveness of the intervention will be analyzed using multilevel analyses. In addition, a process evaluation will assess intervention implementation to help understand why the intervention is effective (or not), and for whom and under which circumstances. Discussion The intervention adopts an interdisciplinary approach, integrating emotion work, sensor-based measurements of physical workload, and quality in early childhood education and care. The study aims to provide theoretical, methodological, and practical insights into how to design and implement a complex intervention in an ECEC setting. Trial registration https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN81684777 , identifier: ISRCTN81684777.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed social media communication by enabling AI systems to produce increasingly human-like language and content. Although research on AI-generated communication and user trust has expanded, findings remain fragmented across platforms, communication contexts, and linguistic characteristics. This study systematically synthesizes empirical evidence on the relationship between AI-generated language and user trust in social media communication. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature was retrieved from the Dimensions database in July 2026 using predefined search terms related to Generative AI, language, trust, and social media. Of 205 records initially identified, 54 full-text studies were assessed for eligibility, and 23 empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. The findings show that research is concentrated in recent years, particularly in marketing and digital communication, health communication, and misinformation and synthetic media. Across the studies, trust is associated with recurring linguistic and communicative features, including human-likeness and conversational style, emotional expression and empathy, personalization, formality and readability, narrative and experiential language, semantic and informational characteristics, transparency and disclosure, and explanatory language. The findings indicate that user trust is not determined by AI authorship alone but emerges through the interaction of relational and epistemic cues within specific communication contexts. This review contributes to human–AI communication research by identifying linguistic and communicative mechanisms through which AI-generated social media content shapes perceptions of trust, credibility, and authenticity.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly being used in clinical practice, yet little is known about how family medicine physicians and trainees explain how these tools work, the challenges they experience, and the support they consider necessary for responsible use. This study qualitatively examined participants’ written descriptions of GenAI across the family medicine training continuum. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted among 87 participants across the family medicine training continuum in Israel, including medical students in family medicine rotations ( n = 28), interns ( n = 13), residents ( n = 16), and specialists or senior physicians ( n = 30). Data were collected through three open-ended prompts embedded in an online Hebrew-language questionnaire. The prompts addressed how GenAI produces responses, challenges associated with its use, and support needed for effective and responsible use. Written responses were analyzed thematically using ATLAS.ti. The analysis remained close to explicitly stated content because the brief written responses did not permit probing or follow-up. Coding was non-exclusive, and all 87 participants provided a usable response to each prompt. Information-aggregation descriptions were identified in 58 participants’ responses (66.7%), and 44 participants (50.6%) likened GenAI to a search engine. Only 10 participants (11.5%) explicitly mentioned probabilistic text generation. Output trustworthiness was the most frequently coded concern: 39 participants (44.8%) mentioned accuracy or reliability, and 20 (23.0%) mentioned hallucinations or fabricated information. Regarding support needs, GenAI literacy and source verification were each mentioned by 18 participants (20.7%), followed by formal training ( n = 10, 11.5%) and access to medical-specific GenAI tools ( n = 9, 10.3%). Because coding was non-exclusive, the counts overlap and should be interpreted descriptively. These findings point to a possible need for targeted GenAI literacy education within family medicine training programs, for clinical governance frameworks, and for GenAI tools that meet the evidentiary standards of medical practice. Because the material consists of brief written answers, these are implications generated by an exploratory sample rather than established requirements.

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the synergies between Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and the emerging paradigm of Construction 6.0, emphasizing the integration of advanced automation with human creativity. As the AEC industry transitions from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0. This chapter highlights how collaborative intelligencesupported by Artificial Intelligence, cobots, Extended Reality/Augmented Reality/Mixed Reality, digital twins, and generative designenables augmented decision-making, adaptive workflows, and safer construction environments. Construction 6.0 builds upon hyper-automation, human-digital ecosystems, and Artificial Intelligence-driven sustainability, introducing technologies such as human-digital twins, immersive interfaces, and predictive analytics to create regenerative, resilient built environments. Ethical considerationsincluding transparency, explainability, algorithmic fairness, data privacy, and human autonomyare identified as essential for trustworthy adoption. The chapter also underscores workforce transformation through reskilling, upskilling, and extended reality-based immersive training. Collectively, these elements position Construction 6.0 as a human-centered, ethically governed, and innovation-driven evolution of the built environment.

This chapter presents a comprehensive framework for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence in Construction 6.0, outlining how Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, and predictive risk modeling integrate to enhance safety and risk management across the project lifecycle. The chapter emphasizes that safety evolves from reactive compliance to a continuous, data-driven, and worker-empowering ecosystem, supported by structured safety information such as ISO 19650-6:2025. Computer Vision enables real-time hazard detectionranging from personal protective equipment compliance to contextual riskthrough edge-based inference, transformers, and emerging vision-language models capable of rule-aware reasoning. NLP unlocks insights from near-miss reports, daily logs, and incident narratives, transforming unstructured text into structured risk intelligence linked to Building Information Modeling/Digital Twin environments. Predictive analytics leverage historical and real-time telemetry to forecast risk hotspots and inform proactive mitigation. Across all technologies, the chapter underscores human-centric design, explainability, ethical governance, and lifecycle integration as essential for trustworthy, resilient safety ecosystems.

This chapter examines how Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence is transforming sustainable and resilient design in the built environment. With buildings responsible for nearly 40% of global energy use and 30% of greenhouse gas emissions, the chapter underscores the need for energy-efficient and carbon-neutral architectural solutions. Human-centric AI integrates explainable Artificial Intelligence, human-in-the-loop decision-making, and participatory design to ensure transparency, ethical alignment, and user-driven sustainability. Artificial Intelligence-enabled predictive energy optimization, reinforcement learning heating ventilation air conditioning control, and digital twinbased lifecycle carbon assessment significantly reduce operational and embodied carbon. In parallel, generative design and parametric modeling support climate-adaptive strategiesfrom passive cooling and flood-resilient layouts to low-carbon material selection. The chapter also highlights Artificial Intelligence-driven infrastructure risk modeling, combining hazard prediction, multi-hazard simulation, and scenario-based planning to enhance resilience. Collectively, these approaches position human-centric Artificial Intelligence as essential for achieving net-zero, adaptive, and resource-efficient built environments.

Agentic artificial intelligence can decompose legal objectives, retrieve authorities, invoke external tools, draft documents, communicate with stakeholders, and execute multi-step workflows. In high-risk legal settings, a final approval click is not an adequate control: errors can propagate across a trajectory, evidence can be withheld from the reviewer, confidential data can cross an unauthorized boundary, and a human may be asked to approve an artifact that no longer matches the version later executed. This paper proposes Human-in-the-Loop Control for Legal Agents (HILC-Legal), a riskadaptive governance architecture that separates language generation from authorization and separates authorization from execution. The architecture combines hard policy constraints, a calibrated action-risk score, evidence packets, competenceaware reviewer routing, version-bound authorization tokens, a least-privilege execution broker, provenance logging, and post-action monitoring. We define six control invariants for legally consequential agent behavior and a four-tier oversight policy ranging from bounded read-only assistance to human-in-command decision making. We also specify an evaluation protocol covering unsafe action escape, authority and evidence fidelity, confidentiality preservation, approval-version consistency, reviewer correction yield, automation bias, workload, calibration, and recovery. The proposal is a design and evaluation framework; it does not claim deployment results. Its central argument is that meaningful human oversight is an engineered control property - requiring information, competence, authority, time, and effective intervention mechanisms - rather than the mere presence of a person in a workflow.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has made it increasingly difficult to distinguish AI-generated and AI-rephrased text from authentic human writing, posing serious risks to academic integrity, journalism, and e-commerce credibility. This paper presents a rigorous benchmark evaluation for three-way AI text origin classification designed to detect human-written, AI-generated, and AI-rephrased text by integrating handcrafted linguistic features, transformer-based contextual embeddings, and ensemble learning strategies. A corpus of 161,788 samples is curated from Amazon product reviews and Twitter posts, with AI-generated text produced via zero-shot prompting and AI-rephrased text produced via few-shot prompting using GPT, DeepSeek, and Kimi. The corpus comprises 46,844 human-written, 57,247 AI-generated, and 57,697 AI-rephrased samples distributed across training (113,249), validation (16,180), and test (32,359) splits. A hybrid feature vector of 168 dimensions is constructed, combining 68 handcrafted stylistic, lexical, linguistic, syntactic, and stylometric features with 100-dimensional embeddings derived from RoBERTa and the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Sentence Transformer. Classical machine learning models, Random Forest, SVM, and Logistic Regression, are trained on this hybrid representation, while RoBERTa-base and DeBERTa-v3-base are fine-tuned end-to-end on raw tokenized text. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that transformer models substantially outperform classical methods, with RoBERTa achieving 95.49% accuracy and DeBERTa-v3 achieving 94.88%. A probability-averaging ensemble further improves accuracy to 95.66%, and a stacking ensemble with a Random Forest meta-learner reaches 96.46%. Ablation studies confirm the complementary value of handcrafted features alongside contextual embeddings. Across all models, AI-rephrased content is the most challenging category due to its semantic proximity to human writing, highlighting a persistent frontier for future research. The dataset and evaluation framework provide a reproducible foundation for future AI content detection research, with generalization to unseen generators and domains identified as primary directions for future work.

Abstract Blockchain technology and artificial intelligence (AI) were introduced and integrated to develop new possibilities for security, automation, and transparency in digital financial ecosystems. This study proposes a hybrid AI Blockchain framework for automated credit evaluation and identity tokenization, addressing issues with opacity, bias, and data manipulation that affect conventional, centralized credit scoring systems. To predict client creditworthiness from past financial behavior, we trained several supervised machine learning models on the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset. These models included Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, KNN, and Gradient Boosting. Support Vector Machine (SVM) outperformed the others in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Their performance metrics ranged between 0.841–0.915 for accuracy, 0.830–0.902 for precision, 0.828–0.900 for recall, and 0.829–0.901 for F1-score. Among all models evaluated, the Random Forest (RF) classifier performed best, achieving an accuracy of 0.907, a precision of 0.895, a recall of 0.894, and an F1-score of 0.895. Ensemble methods, however, achieved higher scores overall; among all seven classifiers, XGBoost obtained the highest raw accuracy (0.915), while Random Forest (RF) was selected as the deployed model, achieving an accuracy of 0.907, a precision of 0.895, a recall of 0.894, and an F1-score of 0.895. Random Forest was preferred over both SVM and XGBoost for production integration because it combined near-top predictive performance with substantially lower training/inference latency, native feature-importance interpretability, and simpler on-chain integration properties that matter for a system whose decisions must be auditable and re-verifiable. RF demonstrated an excellent balance of predictive accuracy, generalization, robustness to overfitting, and interpretability, making it the optimal choice for deployment in the blockchain ecosystem. The Random Forest model’s decisions were integrated into an Ethereum-based smart contract, which issues non-transferable identity tokens to qualified users and permanently records loan approval results. By providing verifiable audit trails, tamper resistance, and transparency, this blockchain layer increases confidence in decentralized financial (DeFi) services. Experimental findings confirm the hybrid architecture’s sustainability, scalability, and dependability. These findings focus on model accuracy and on-chain execution cost; broader claims about fairness and governance impact are discussed as architectural potential rather than measured outcomes. According to the study, AI-enhanced smart contracts can significantly enhance the security, accountability, and fairness of financial decision-making while providing a framework for future applications in supply chain management, healthcare, and decentralized identity management. Consistent with the scope described above, the fairness and governance benefits discussed here reflect the architecture’s design potential rather than experimentally demonstrated outcomes.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Space heating load is the main energy consumption driver for residential buildings, and its estimation is critical for the efficient and economic operation of energy systems. In this paper, nine different Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Machine Learning (ML) models — Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), Elastic Net (ENet), Extreme Learning Machine (ELM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Decision Tree (DT), Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (HGB), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and a hybrid Autoencoder and Deep Extreme Learning Machine (AE + DELM) — are compared to estimate space heating load using seven independent input variables. The comparison is mainly carried out using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R 2 ), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). Additionally, Residual Prediction Deviation (RPD) and uncertainty analysis using the prediction interval coverage percentage (p-factor) and the normalized prediction interval width (d-factor) are employed to further confirm the findings. The hybrid AE + DELM method demonstrates superior performance among all modelling approaches and achieves the lowest MAPE value of 0.04. The excellent performance of the hybrid AE + DELM model is further demonstrated by its high RPD, while all models show strong correlations with R 2 scores above 0.99. Although CNN and XGBoost also exhibit strong performance, LSTM and HGB show comparatively higher uncertainty.

Breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent health challenges affecting women worldwide, yet gaps in breast health literacy continue to hinder early detection and informed healthcare decision-making.In the era of Society 5.0, where technology is increasingly designed to serve human needs, artificial intelligence presents new opportunities to transform health education into a more accessible, engaging, and empowering experience.This plenary session introduces the Breast Imaging Education Bot (BieBot), a human-centric artificial intelligence (AI) initiative developed to enhance breast health literacy and promote proactive health behaviours among communities.Designed as a bilingual conversational chatbot, BieBot provides evidence-based information on breast cancer awareness, risk factors, screening options, and breast self-examination through an interactive and user-friendly digital platform.By integrating educational content, multimedia resources, instructional videos, and direct access to screening-related services, the initiative seeks to bridge knowledge gaps while improving access to reliable health information.The presentation will showcase the development journey of BieBot, highlighting how human-centred design principles, stakeholder engagement, and healthcare expertise were combined to create a meaningful digital health solution.Community evaluation findings reveal high levels of user acceptance, demonstrating the chatbot's effectiveness in supporting self-directed learning and increasing awareness of breast health practices.Furthermore, the initiative illustrates the potential of AI-powered health education to extend beyond awareness campaigns by fostering empowerment, informed decision-making, and greater participation in preventive healthcare.By sharing the BieBot experience, this session offers a practical example of how human-centric AI can be leveraged to create inclusive, scalable, and impactful healthcare innovations.The discussion will provide valuable insights for healthcare professionals, educators, researchers, and policymakers seeking to harness emerging technologies to improve health literacy and strengthen community wellbeing in the digital age.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has become a highly transformative technology with the capacity to reshape teaching and learning in schools and other educational institutions.Since it can facilitate intelligent content generation, adaptive learning, automated assessment, and personalized instructional support, Generative AI provides numerous opportunities for improving the quality of education, increasing learner engagement, and boosting instructional efficiency.This paper gives a critical look at the effect of Generative AI on teaching and learning by looking at its applications, advantages, challenges, and future potential in the education sector.The study looks at major opportunities such as personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, content creation, and collaborative learning environments, while also tackling important issues like algorithmic opacity, explainability, data privacy and security, bias and fairness, academic integrity, and the reliability of content produced by AI.The paper also examines ways of responsibly introducing Generative AI by creating transparent and ethical AI frameworks, establishing strong data governance mechanisms, setting up appropriate regulatory policies, and using high-quality training datasets.It stresses the need to give teachers the necessary AI skills through ongoing professional development so that they can effectively incorporate AI-based teaching methods.Lastly, the study highlights some of the new trends in AI-driven education, such as intelligent tutoring systems, immersive virtual learning environments, adaptive assessment, and collaborative human-AI learning ecosystems.The results show that although Generative AI offers great potential for enhancing educational accessibility, personalization, and learning outcomes, its successful implementation relies on ethical governance, responsible use, and continued cooperation between educators, researchers, policymakers, and technology developers.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Water cycle education at the elementary school level often faces challenges due to abstract concept visualization, causing students to memorize text without understanding real-world environmental dynamics. This community service initiative aims to deliver interactive water cycle learning at SD N Bronggang Baru using a modern multimedia ecosystem. The program was carried out through technology implementation followed by mentoring and evaluation phases. The participants included 28 fifth-grade students and a companion teacher, utilizing the school’s multimedia room. The implemented multimedia ecosystem combines Google Veo AI-based animated videos, Google Gemini AI-based educational games, and a web GIS platform. The results demonstrate that integrating artificial intelligence and web GIS significantly boosts student enthusiasm and active classroom participation. The final evaluation shows clear progress in student comprehension; they are now able to fully understand hydrological processes while connecting atmospheric phenomena with field-level groundwater conditions. Furthermore, students' critical thinking skills were enhanced through their active involvement in formulating solutions to local environmental issues. This program recommends replicating similar applied community service projects to strengthen spatial and disaster literacy in primary education.Abstrak: Pembelajaran materi siklus air di tingkat sekolah dasar sering kali menghadapi kendala visualisasi konsep yang abstrak, sehingga siswa cenderung menghafal secara tekstual tanpa memahami dinamika lingkungan nyata. Kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan untuk melaksanakan pembelajaran siklus air yang interaktif di SD N Bronggang Baru menggunakan ekosistem multimedia modern. Metode pelaksanaan dilakukan melalui penerapan teknologi serta pendampingan dan evaluasi. Sasaran kegiatan melibatkan 28 siswa kelas 5 dan guru pendamping, bertempat di ruang multimedia sekolah. Ekosistem multimedia yang diimplementasikan mengombinasikan video animasi berbasis AI Google Veo, permainan edukatif berbasis AI Google Gemini, dan platform web GIS . Hasil pelaksanaan menunjukkan bahwa integrasi teknologi kecerdasan buatan dan web GIS secara signifikan mampu meningkatkan antusiasme dan partisipasi aktif siswa di kelas. Evaluasi akhir menunjukkan perkembangan nyata pada pemahaman siswa, yang kini mampu memahami proses hidrologi secara utuh sekaligus mengaitkan fenomena atmosfer dengan kondisi air tanah di lapangan. Kemampuan berpikir kritis siswa juga terasah melalui keaktifan dalam merumuskan solusi atas masalah lingkungan di sekitar mereka. Program ini merekomendasikan replikasi pengabdian terapan sejenis untuk penguatan literasi spasial dan kebencanaan pada pendidikan dasar.

Abstrak: Kegiatan pengabdian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh kebutuhan penguatan kompetensi digital guru sekolah dasar serta kebutuhan alternatif pembelajaran yang lebih fleksibel pada sekolah mitra yang menghadapi gangguan pembelajaran akibat banjir musiman. Kegiatan bertujuan meningkatkan kompetensi digital guru melalui implementasi LMS LENTERA 101752 serta pelatihan pengembangan media berbantuan Generative AI dan Augmented Reality (AR). Kegiatan dilaksanakan melalui pelatihan dan workshop dengan mitra guruSD Negeri di, Kabupaten Deli Serdang, yang melibatkan 21 guru. Evaluasi dilakukan melalui observasi selama kegiatan serta pre-test dan post-test kompetensi digital. Data pre-test dan post-test dianalisis secara deskriptif dengan membandingkan nilai rata-rata sebelum dan sesudah kegiatan, menghitung selisih peningkatan nilai dan persentase peningkatan, serta menentukan proporsi peserta yang mengalami peningkatan nilai Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan rata-rata nilai meningkat dari 62,11 menjadi 82,63 atau meningkat 20,53 poin (33,05%) dengan N-gain 0,54 (kategori sedang) dan 94,74% peserta mengalami peningkatan nilai. Kegiatan memberikan progres positif terhadap kompetensi digital guru dalam memanfaatkan LMS, Generative AI, dan AR untuk mendukung pengembangan pembelajaran yang lebih fleksibel dan interaktif.Abstract: This community engagement program was motivated by the need to strengthen elementary school teachers’ digital competence and provide more flexible learning alternatives in a partner school affected by seasonal flooding. The program aimed to improve teachers’ digital competence through the implementation of the LENTERA 101752 Learning Management System (LMS) and training in developing learning media using Generative AI and Augmented Reality (AR). The activities were conducted through training and workshops involving 21 teachers from a public elementary school in Deli Serdang Regency. Evaluation was conducted through observation during the activities, as well as pre-test and post-test assessments of teachers’ digital competence. The data were analyzed descriptively by comparing the mean scores before and after the activities, calculating the difference and percentage increase, and determining the proportion of participants whose scores improved. The evaluation results showed that the mean score increased from 62.11 to 82.63, representing an increase of 20.53 points (33.05%), with an N-gain of 0.54 (moderate category), and 94.74% of participants showing an improvement in their scores. The program demonstrated positive progress in teachers’ digital competence in utilizing LMS, Generative AI, and AR to support more flexible and interactive learning.

Background Drug-related harm is a major global public health concern, with opioids implicated in over 70% of drug-related deaths. Scotland reports the highest drug-related mortality rate in Europe, with remote and rural communities facing additional barriers to accessing harm reduction and treatment services. Assertive outreach is increasingly recognised as a key strategy to engage individuals at risk who are disconnected from traditional services. This study evaluates the use of a Trigger Checklist to identify and outreach individuals within 48 hours of referral in a rural Emergency Department (ED). Methods A realist evaluation explored how and why the Trigger Checklist works within the complexity of an ED setting. Guided by Pawson and Tilley’s framework, the evaluation followed three stages: theory gleaning, refining, and consolidation. Initial programme theories were developed using literature and advisory group input, then refined through 13 realist interviews with ED clinicians and outreach workers (OW). Data were analysed using Context-Mechanism-Outcome (CMO) configurations and linked to middle-range theories. Results Three programme theories emerged: (1) Confident decision-making, where certainty, conversational aids, ethical reasoning, and outreach worker prompts influenced checklist use; (2) Trusting relationships, shaped by OWs’ approachability, situational awareness, and mutual respect; and (3) Perceived value, driven by altruism, narrative feedback, and perceived reductions in ED visits. Relational coordination theory explained how shared goals, knowledge, and respect – reinforced by timely, accurate communication – enabled coordinated action. OW presence and recovery discussions were critical to foster confident and appropriate referrals among ED clinicians. Conclusions The Trigger Checklist can support timely outreach potentially reducing drug-related harm in rural ED settings, but its success depends on relational dynamics, perceived value, and organisational integration. To avoid checklist fatigue or tokenistic use, it should be embedded with the support of OWs who foster trust. These relationships will enhance use of the checklist as a meaningful intervention within complex care systems.

Abstract Given that deepfake videos are now easy to generate and increasingly high in quality, the present research investigated human detection performance and several routes to improvement. Across four experiments, participants demonstrated above-chance detection accuracy when viewing YouTube clips and their corresponding deepfakes, but performance remained modest and error-prone. In Experiment 1, aggregating responses across the full sample produced reliable improvements in accuracy, consistent with a ‘wisdom of the crowd’ effect. However, in Experiment 2, participants showed no evidence of metacognitive sensitivity. Although confidence was modestly higher for correct than incorrect decisions, it did not reliably discriminate between them at the trial level. Consistent with this finding, confidence-weighted fusion of participant pairs reduced rather than improved accuracy. In Experiments 3 and 4, we examined human–AI collaboration, with participants making decisions before and after receiving simulated algorithmic guidance. Performance improved following guidance when it was highly accurate, but this benefit was offset by a tendency to follow incorrect advice when it occurred. Notably, this reliance on simulated algorithmic guidance was unaffected by the prevalence of deepfakes within the stimulus set. Taken together, these findings suggest that, while both aggregation and human–AI collaboration can enhance performance under certain conditions, their effectiveness is constrained by poor metacognitive insight and a general tendency to align decisions with external advice. Improving deepfake detection may depend not only on advances in algorithmic performance, but also on a better understanding of how humans interpret and use both perceptual and algorithmic information.

documents.abstract: This study investigated the impact of a problem-solving instructional strategy on the interest of senior secondary school students in mathematics in Kaduna State, Nigeria. Rooted in Self-Determination Theory, which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as drivers of intrinsic motivation, the research employed a quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test control group design. A total of 204 SS2 students from three public schools were assigned to either an experimental group, which was taught using a structured problem-solving strategy, or a control group, which was instructed via conventional methods. Students’ interest in mathematics was assessed using a validated adaptation of the Mathematics Interest Questionnaire (MIQ). Data were analysed using ANCOVA to control for baseline differences. Results indicated a statistically significant positive effect of the problem-solving strategy on students’ post-test interest scores (F(1, 130) = 13.590, p < .001, η² = .095), affirming the hypothesis that learner-centred, inquiry-driven instruction fosters greater affective engagement than traditional approaches. These findings underscore the role of problem-solving in stimulating psychological engagement and enhancing the affective domain in mathematics learning. The study contributes to the broader literature advocating for pedagogical reforms that prioritise active learning, especially within under-resourced and socio-culturally diverse educational contexts. Implications for theory, policy, and instructional practice are discussed, alongside recommendations for future research into long-term and demographic-specific effects of problem-solving pedagogy.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being introduced into clinical environments, but their influence on physician decision-making, particularly when responses are incorrect, remains insufficiently understood. The aim of the study was to assess whether pediatricians are influenced by LLM-generated answers in their clinical decision-making and whether they can distinguish correct from incorrect AI-generated responses. Ninety-eight pediatrician participants were recruited through convenience sampling from university hospitals and private clinics in Greece between February and July 2025. Mixed-effects logistic regression models were used to compare differences in participant behavior when the LLM provided correct versus incorrect answers. The main outcomes were the ability of pediatricians to distinguish correct from incorrect LLM-generated answers and the extent to which AI-generated responses influenced changes in their clinical decisions. Subgroup analyses evaluated differences by training level and practice setting. Among 98 pediatricians, most were able to distinguish between correct and incorrect LLM-generated answers using their clinical experience and training ( p < 0.001). Overall, most participants were able to use LLM output constructively without being misled by incorrect responses. Most pediatricians retained the ability to recognize incorrect LLM-generated information and were able to use LLMs as supportive diagnostic tools. However, pediatric residents ( p = 0.02) and private-practice pediatricians ( p = 0.005) were more likely to change their answers based on AI-generated responses, even when the LLM-provided answer was incorrect. The greater susceptibility of residents and private-practice pediatricians to incorrect LLM output suggests a risk of authority or priming effects. These findings support the need for targeted training and implementation safeguards before widespread clinical deployment of LLMs in pediatric practice.

documents.abstract: Fluorescent immunohistochemistry tissue imaging is an important tool for studying brain structure, neuronal activity, and molecular expression within anatomically defined regions. In hippocampal research, region-specific analysis is particularly important because hippocampal subregions have distinct structural and functional roles in memory, plasticity, and neurological disease. Automated segmentation, semantic identification, and cellular quantification of these tissue images therefore represent important problems in computational neuroscience and biomedical image analysis. Despite advances in deep learning-based biomedical image analysis, automated analysis of hippocampal fluorescent immunohistochemistry images remains challenging. Existing methods primarily focus on generic medical image segmentation, MRI-based hippocampal analysis, or cell-level detection without explicitly modeling hippocampal subregion structure. Consequently, integrated computational frameworks that segment hippocampal subregions, identify them semantically, and quantify cells within anatomically meaningful boundaries remain limited. Limited annotated datasets, heterogeneous staining patterns, low signal-to-noise ratio, dense cellular organization, and variability in manual annotations further complicate reliable and scalable analysis. This dissertation addresses these challenges through a progressive three-stage computational framework. In parallel, we introduce annotated murine hippocampal tissue image datasets across multiple staining modalities, providing benchmark resources for subregion-level analysis and cellular quantification. First, we introduce ROIsGAN, a region-guided generative adversarial framework that combines a U-Net-based generator with a region-guided discriminator that provides spatially informed adversarial supervision to encourage anatomically consistent hippocampal subregion segmentation under heterogeneous staining conditions. Next, we present MT-UGAN, which extends segmentation to semantic region identification through multitask learning. Using a shared encoder and task-specific output heads, it jointly segments and classifies hippocampal subregions, capturing structural and semantic information while assigning labels such as dentate gyrus, CA1, and CA3. Finally, we introduce FM-SAM for region-specific cellular analysis through cell-level instance segmentation and counting in fluorescent microscopy images. The framework adapts the Segment Anything Model to hippocampal immunohistochemistry through domain-specific fine-tuning and automated prompt generation, enabling automated cell quantification within anatomically defined subregions and supporting downstream biological analysis. Overall, this dissertation establishes an integrated framework that progresses from subregion segmentation to semantic identification and region-specific cellular quantification. The proposed methods and datasets support scalable, reproducible, and biologically meaningful analysis of fluorescent immunohistochemistry images while reducing reliance on manual analysis.

The global textile industry is based on cotton, which supports millions of livelihoods, yet it is becoming increasingly threatened by increasing pest pressures and global climate change. Increased temperatures, high levels of CO2 and changing rainfall distribution are changing pest biology, geographic distributions, and relationships with crops and natural enemies. These alterations increase pest and disease outbreaks, exert selective pressure in favor of resistant strains of pests and vectors of arboviruses and undermine the efficacy of traditional chemical and biological control. Meanwhile, continued declines in pollinators pose an additional risk to yields and the quality of fibers. Thus, the conventional pesticide-based control will lead to resistance, environmental degradation, and human health hazards and is no longer sufficient in climate-stressed cotton regimes. Research, encourages climate-intelligent (IPM), combining resistant or climate-tolerant crops, diversified crop regimes, natural enemy conservation, and sophisticated monitoring and modelling technologies, such as remote sensing and artificial intelligence (AI). IPM integrates cultural, mechanical, biological, and judicious chemical strategies, yet must adapt to the fast-changing pest dynamics. The chapter discusses the applications of sensors, diagnostic algorithms, predictive models, and smart traps that are sensitive AI based system, that could enable early identification of pests, diseases, and nutrient stress, supporting precise, timely intervention and the need for broad-spectrum pesticides. An IPM-AI model specific to cotton, based on fieldwork on the most important pests under changing climatic conditions, will enhance real-time monitoring, diagnostic capabilities, and decision support. It is a combined strategy to improve pest control, protect the yield and farm revenues, and sustain and enhance the resilience of cotton production in the face of rising climatic variability.

This research investigates the impact of artificial intelligence on contemporary training systems, emphasizing its function in providing individualized learning, increasing interest in tasks, and offering instantaneous feedback. It also analyzes the notable advantages AI offers for organizational workforce development alongside the challenges such as organizational ethics and privacy, data security, bias, and transparency. The study observes the need to integrate human intuition with AI technology, emphasizing the importance of thoughtfully designed frameworks that effectively harness training AI while ensuring inclusivity. Lastly, the author presents suggestions for organizational policies that wish to incorporate AI technologies into training programs in a manner that responsibly prepares them for future workplace challenges.

Digitalisation and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) will reshape sustainable materials engineering by enabling data-driven design and performance prediction for smart infrastructure. In this study, experimental durability assessment and machine learning techniques were combined to investigate silica fume (SF) and ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBFS)-based UHPC subjected to normal curing (NC), steam curing (SC), and wrapped curing (WC). Mechanical, durability, and mineralogical characterisation tests were performed, including compressive strength, the Rapid Chloride Penetration Test (RCPT), water absorption, sorptivity, an accelerated corrosion test, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Accelerated steam curing (SC) produced a measured early-age compressive strength of 85.97 MPa at 6 h and the lowest RCPT value of 81.09 Coulombs among the investigated curing conditions. The measured water absorption and accelerated corrosion results also varied with curing conditions, with SC showing comparatively favourable performance. These findings provide experimental evidence of curing-dependent mechanical and durability behaviour, although the pore structure was not directly quantified. XRD analysis provided qualitative evidence of differences in the crystalline and amorphous features of the UHPC matrix under the investigated curing conditions. An exploratory comparison of compressive strength and chloride-ion penetrability was performed; however, the measurements were obtained at different curing ages and from only three experimental curing conditions, so no age-matched or quantitative strength–RCPT relationship was established. An XGBoost model (R2 = 0.9591) was developed using the adopted dataset and 80/20 test partition to support digital materials engineering. SHAP-based feature attribution identified SF, curing age, superplasticizer dosage, and fibre reinforcement as important model features for compressive-strength prediction. The combined experimental–XAI framework enables a qualitative consistency assessment between observed UHPC behaviour and data-driven feature attribution. Because the experimental specimens were independent of the ML database, the experimental programme serves as a qualitative consistency check of SHAP-based feature attribution rather than a rigorous validation of the model predictions.

Plant biosensor engineering currently relies on empirical, single-target strategies, limiting predictability and scalability. This review presents a comprehensive, data-driven framework that integrates multi-omics, machine learning, and synthetic biology to enable rational biosensor design. A systematic analysis of 1,548 peer-reviewed publications (2020–2026) reveals exponential growth—from 90 papers in 2020 to 646 in 2026 (7.2-fold increase)—with 70% of the corpus published between 2024 and 2026. An additional 40 pre-2020 foundational references are included in the full validated bibliography of 1,588 records. Bibliometric clustering identifies three major research poles: molecular sensors, omics integration, and AI-driven design. Analysis of real multi-omics datasets (GSE206890, PXD024902, PXD030428, PXD072721) from Arabidopsis, rice, and maize consistently shows up-regulation of ABA signaling, reactive oxygen species metabolism, and transcription factor networks. Building on these findings, the authors propose PlantBioSense-DF, a modular ten-step architecture covering data acquisition, quality control, harmonization, feature engineering, machine learning, explainable AI (SHAP, LIME), biomarker discovery, and synthetic biology circuit design. The framework prioritizes interpretable biomarkers for direct translation to engineering. Key challenges addressed include data heterogeneity, batch effects, model interpretability, and laboratory-to-field transfer. Future directions highlight digital twins, foundation models, graph AI, and single-cell/spatial omics integration. Together, this work offers a systematic, evidence-based roadmap for accelerating plant biosensor development through predictive, data-driven approaches. All analysis scripts and processed data will be made publicly available to ensure reproducibility and foster community adoption of the framework.

Polymeric nanofluids have emerged as advanced multifunctional materials with significant potential in thermal management, energy systems, biomedical engineering, advanced manufacturing, and smart-material applications. Their performance is governed by complex interfacial interactions between nanoparticles and polymer matrices, which influence colloidal stability, rheological behavior, thermal transport, electrical conductivity, and long-term durability. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamental interfacial science, structure–property relationships, and functional performance mechanisms governing polymeric nanofluids. Particular emphasis is placed on nanoparticle–polymer interactions, surface functionalization strategies, interphase formation, microstructural evolution, rheo-chemical coupling, thermal transport pathways, and electrokinetic phenomena. The review further highlights the application of advanced characterization techniques, especially ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and chemometric analysis, for elucidating molecular interactions and establishing quantitative structure–property correlations. Recent developments in machine learning, materials informatics, response surface methodology, and digital-twin frameworks are critically discussed as transformative tools for predictive modeling, formulation optimization, and real-time adaptive control. Key findings indicate that interfacial architecture and microstructural organization are the primary determinants of multifunctional performance, while data-driven approaches significantly accelerate materials discovery and optimization. Emerging directions involving stimuli-responsive nanofluids, artificial-intelligence-assisted design, sustainable formulations, and autonomous monitoring systems are also explored. By integrating molecular-level understanding with advanced analytical and computational approaches, this review establishes a unified framework for the rational design of intelligent, high-performance polymeric nanofluids and identifies future opportunities for their large-scale implementation in energy, environmental, biomedical, and industrial technologies.

Background: Recent studies of Nepalese male migrant workers in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Malaysia have highlighted substantial health risks, with many cardiovascular-related deaths reported as sudden cardiac deaths. Most such deaths are not adequately investigated. This study explored (a) the circumstances surrounding these deaths and (b) potential contributing factors. Method and Materials: Following public and patient involvement and engagement (PPIE) activities with key stakeholders and Nepalese migrant communities in Malaysia, we conducted a verbal autopsy study of 57 friends, roommates, and relatives of 40 Nepali nationals who had died unexpectedly in Malaysia. Results: Most of the deceased were men (92.5%, n=37), with a mean age of 34.5 years (SD 8.3) and a mean duration of employment in Malaysia of 5.9 years (SD 4.4). Only 40.0% (n=16) reportedly received a regular weekly rest day, while 80.0% (n=32) worked more than 8 hours per day. Among those who consumed alcohol (n=33), one-third (33.3%, n=11) drank daily. More than half of the deceased (55.0%, n=22) had at least one pre-existing health condition, most commonly hypertension (32.5%, n=13), followed by diabetes (7.5%, n=3). Conclusion: The circumstances surrounding sudden deaths among Nepalese migrant workers in Malaysia suggest a potential contribution from cardiovascular risk factors, lifestyle behaviours, and adverse working conditions. Reducing this burden will require targeted health-promotion interventions, improved prevention and management of cardiovascular risk factors, stronger occupational health protections, and measures to prevent the production and consumption of counterfeit alcohol.

Introduction The Implicit Situation Intensity Test (ISIT) is a method for converting participants’ verbal reports about an experience into a quantitative, per-participant implicit measure of how strongly cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and value-laden frames have been activated by that experience. Method ISIT operates by clustering frames extracted from the verbal report’s extended knowledge graph (XKG)—the structured representation produced by the POLANYI++ neurosymbolic pipeline—into a Frame Ontology (FO) and scoring each frame’s salience for each participant on a normalized scale. The implicit measure produced by ISIT is designed to be combined with explicit measures from standardized questionnaires, implicit measures from physiological sensors, and participant profile information, in a single multivariate analysis of situated experience, producing participant-level scores , suitable for psychometric integration. Results We illustrate the method through the Lucifora et al. study on virtual male embodiment in a catcalling scenario ( n = 36), in which a 37-indicator Frame Ontology spanning four domains (emotional states, behavioral responses, violence perception, and semantic markers), whose frame clusters entered the study’s multivariate correlation structure alongside the standardized instruments and emotion ratings; safety-related frames showed differential correlation patterns with anger and sadness versus with fear that simpler instruments do not capture. To place the extraction itself on an auditable footing, every frame the pipeline produced was adjudicated by a tacit-aware judge (DEEPJUDGE) and human-verified: frame-level precision on a warrant criterion was high (0.95–0.96 across two foundation-model backends, with near-zero over-projection), and the two backends produced markedly more similar profiles for the same report than for different ones. Discussion ISIT shares with grounded theory (GT) and computational grounded theory (CGT) the inductive commitment that situational structure should emerge from data, but it differs in three operational respects: it operates on structured extended knowledge graphs (XKGs) rather than raw text; it produces participant-level numerical scores rather than corpus-level qualitative themes; and it integrates by design with other measurement channels rather than standing as a free-standing qualitative analysis. ISIT fills the verbal-channel gap in the cognitive-science measurement ecosystem: it is the implicit-measure complement to autonomic, behavioral, and questionnaire-based instruments, not their replacement. Convergent and divergent validity against standard implicit measures, predictive validity against behavioral outcomes, and multi-modal integration validation are set out as a defined roadmap.

We present a data-driven approach for accelerating the discovery of high-performance CoSb₃-based skutterudites by curating a comprehensive dataset of compositions with various filler elements from over 300 research articles. Leveraging large language models (LLMs), we extract and embed compositional representations, which are then used to train a regression head for predicting thermoelectric figure of merit. Compared to conventional neural-network models using one-hot encoding and composition-based feature vector (CBFV) representations, our LLM-based model achieves lower prediction errors, while demonstrating predictive performance comparable to a CBFV-based random forest model. We further employ the trained model to propose novel filler compositions with promising thermoelectric properties. Finally, we support these predicted candidates through density functional theory and molecular dynamics calculations to assess their electrical and thermal conductivity. This data-driven approach demonstrates the potential of combining natural language processing, machine learning, and quantum simulations for thermoelectric materials design.

Background Robotic-assisted microsurgery offers enhanced precision, tremor filtration, and improved ergonomics, but adoption is limited by undefined learning curves. This systematic review evaluates the learning curve of microvascular anastomosis performed on dedicated robotic platforms. Methods A systematic review was conducted across MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane databases (inception to June 2025). Evaluated outcomes included time metrics (anastomosis time, time per stitch), microsurgical skills and anastomosis quality for the robot-assisted (RA) and hand-sewn (HS) techniques. Results After screening 6,743 records, 19 studies were included. In preclinical studies (n=11), mean RA anastomosis time decreased by 18.54 [4.01–47.00] minutes versus 8.43 [0.31–30.00] minutes for HS, although mean final RA time remained longer at the final attempt (20.94 [8.99–36.00] vs 14.78 [4.58–30.00]). RA time per stitch decreased by a mean of 2.96 [0.83–5.62] minutes compared to 1.58 [-0.31–4.84] minutes in the HS group. Preclinical microsurgical skill scores improved by 0.99 [0.50–1.63] in the RA group and by 0.76 [-0.10–1.30] in the HS group. In clinical studies (n=8), RA anastomosis time was reduced by 18.03 [6.30–37.27] minutes over anastomosis attempts. Preclinical Anastomosis Lapse Index scores were comparable between techniques. Reported immediate patency in clinical settings ranged from 95.66% to 100%. Conclusion Performance on dedicated robotic platforms improved with practice, but the current evidence did not demonstrate overall superiority over HS technique. In preclinical studies, final RA anastomosis and per-stitch times remained longer, while early anastomosis quality and patency were broadly comparable. Considering added time and platform-associated costs, the clinical settings in which robotic assistance may provide a meaningful benefit remain to be defined. Heterogeneity in models, operators, platforms, and outcome reporting limits definitive characterization of the learning curve. Future studies should standardize learning curve methodology, report complete sequential trajectories, and define clinically relevant proficiency thresholds before integration into credentialing frameworks.

This educational resource comprises a complete set of 12 lesson plans and accompanying handouts for a course titled "Assessment and Test Construction in Social Sciences Education". The course is designed for third-semester pre-service teachers at Farhangian University, Iran, and is delivered in Persian. The course adopts a blended approach, integrating classical assessment paradigms (e.g., Classical Test Theory, Bloom's Taxonomy, Cronbach's Alpha, Messick's validity framework) with modern AI-era perspectives (e.g., Integrated AI Triad (IAT), Reverse PCK, Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP), Toolprint, Consistency Quotient (CQ), AI-Resistant Tasks, and TVDT). A central innovation is the Human-AI Integration (HAI) framework, which positions AI as a co-thinker rather than a replacement for teacher judgment. The 12 sessions guide students through a complete assessment cycle, from foundational concepts to the design, validation, and publication of a comprehensive assessment package. Each session includes a handout (classical and/or integrated), a lesson plan with operational prompts, and a team-based project milestone. By the end of the course, each team produces a six-component assessment package for a selected lesson from Sociology 1 or 2, and publishes it as an open educational resource on Zenodo. The 12 Sessions Fundamental Concepts of Assessment and the Learning-Assessment Life Cycle – Distinguishing measurement, assessment, evaluation, and test; introducing the six-stage learning-assessment cycle. Classification of Tests and Knowledge Graph – Classical test classification (Sif's ten perspectives); extracting the knowledge graph of a lesson; identifying blind spots and error scenarios. Two-Dimensional Table and Consistency Quotient (CQ) – Designing a Bloom × content table; calculating CQ to measure internal coherence. Attitude Assessment and Task Vulnerability Diagnostic Triad (TVDT) – Likert scales and reliability; analyzing task vulnerability using TVDT. Item Bank and Cognitive Depth (Toolprint) – Bloom's taxonomy and item analysis; introducing Toolprint (Interrogative Density, Interrogative Range, Tool Alignment). Validity, Reliability, and Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP) – CVR, CVI, Cronbach's Alpha; CAP for resolving inter-rater discrepancies. Statistical Analysis of Tests – Classical Test Theory (p, D, item-total correlation) and Item Response Theory (IRT); data-driven analysis with AI. Growth-Oriented Feedback – Hattie & Timperley's three-question model; AI-generated feedback patterns; compassionate feedback. Performance Assessment and Rubric – Authentic assessment and analytic rubrics; AI-Resistant Tasks and four resistance mechanisms. Digital Assessment Infrastructure and Targeted Remediation – Portfolios and digital infrastructure; three-layer remedial redesign (PRC Workshop). Norm-Referenced Tests – Norms, Z-scores, T-scores, stanines; smart norms and computerized adaptive testing (CAT). Presenting the Assessment Package and Publishing in Zenodo – Classical reporting vs. open dissemination; preparing the package for Zenodo with DOI. Intended Audience Teacher educators, pre-service social science teachers, curriculum designers, and researchers in educational assessment. Course Structure 26 teams, each working on one lesson from Sociology 1 or 2 (27 lessons total). Team roles: Documentation Manager (laptop access), Prompt Engineer (AI account control), Qualitative Evaluator (output review). All lesson plans and handouts are in Persian.

Each session includes a handout (classical and/or integrated), a lesson plan with operational prompts, and a team-based project milestone. By the end of the course, each team produces a six-component assessment package for a selected lesson from Sociology 1 or 2, and publishes it as an open educational resource on Zenodo. The 12 Sessions Fundamental Concepts of Assessment and the Learning-Assessment Life Cycle – Distinguishing measurement, assessment, evaluation, and test; introducing the six-stage learning-assessment cycle. Classification of Tests and Knowledge Graph – Classical test classification (Sif's ten perspectives); extracting the knowledge graph of a lesson; identifying blind spots and error scenarios. Two-Dimensional Table and Consistency Quotient (CQ) – Designing a Bloom × content table; calculating CQ to measure internal coherence. Attitude Assessment and Task Vulnerability Diagnostic Triad (TVDT) – Likert scales and reliability; analyzing task vulnerability using TVDT. Item Bank and Cognitive Depth (Toolprint) – Bloom's taxonomy and item analysis; introducing Toolprint (Interrogative Density, Interrogative Range, Tool Alignment). Validity, Reliability, and Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP) – CVR, CVI, Cronbach's Alpha; CAP for resolving inter-rater discrepancies. Statistical Analysis of Tests – Classical Test Theory (p, D, item-total correlation) and Item Response Theory (IRT); data-driven analysis with AI. Growth-Oriented Feedback – Hattie & Timperley's three-question model; AI-generated feedback patterns; compassionate feedback. Performance Assessment and Rubric – Authentic assessment and analytic rubrics; AI-Resistant Tasks and four resistance mechanisms. Digital Assessment Infrastructure and Targeted Remediation – Portfolios and digital infrastructure; three-layer remedial redesign (PRC Workshop). Norm-Referenced Tests – Norms, Z-scores, T-scores, stanines; smart norms and computerized adaptive testing (CAT). Presenting the Assessment Package and Publishing in Zenodo – Classical reporting vs. open dissemination; preparing the package for Zenodo with DOI. Intended Audience Teacher educators, pre-service social science teachers, curriculum designers, and researchers in educational assessment. Course Structure 26 teams, each working on one lesson from Sociology 1 or 2 (27 lessons total). Team roles: Documentation Manager (laptop access), Prompt Engineer (AI account control), Qualitative Evaluator (output review). All lesson plans and handouts are in Persian.

Shipping is a critical industry for global trade but is associated with environmental externalities like air, underwater noise, and light pollution. Transitioning to a sustainable future requires optimizing propulsion systems, which currently suffer from fossil fuel reliance and energy losses. This research develops an AI-assisted evidence-synthesis framework to examine sustainable shipping and propulsion technologies and support a policy framework for a sustainable maritime agenda. The study maps how engineering and policy research align across post-2005 literature. The findings demonstrate that sustainability is explicitly multi-dimensional and cannot be reduced to emissions alone. By normalizing and comparing concept intensities across technical and policy-oriented corpora, this study uncovers significant gaps in literature attention. Specifically, propulsion-specific engineering heavily emphasizes electrification and noise reduction, whereas policy discourse focuses primarily on emissions and renewable energy targets. This structured mapping provides academia and practice with a modular decision-support framework to identify topic misalignments, track temporal theme variations, and enhance policy monitoring. Furthermore, these contributions directly support multiple United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including SDGs 7, 9, 12, 13, 14, and 17. The proposed AI-assisted workflow serves as a transparent sense-making mechanism adaptable to other industries undergoing sustainability-driven technological transitions.

As digital technologies increasingly redefine teaching and learning practices, artificial intelligence tools such as Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (ChatGPT) have emerged as pivotal innovations capable of transforming pedagogy. By leveraging advanced natural language processing, ChatGPT enables interactive, personalized, and responsive learning experiences, making it particularly relevant in disciplines like accounting education where both conceptual understanding and practical application are essential. This paper examines leveraging the potential of Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer in pedagogical applications in Accounting Education in tertiary institutions Nigerian. The study addresses the emergence of ChatGPT, concept of pedagogy, pedagogical value of ChatGPT, teaching and learning challenges in accounting education, pedagogical applications of ChatGPT in accounting education and maintaining ethical pedagogy in accounting education. It recommends targeted capacity building for lecturers, development of AI-aligned curriculum guidelines, institutional regulation of AI-supported assessments, and structured integration of ChatGPT to support learner engagement, conceptual mastery, and digital competence.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract AI is increasingly incorporated into psychiatric triage, risk prediction, passive monitoring, clinical documentation, and patient-facing conversational systems. These applications may improve access, continuity, efficiency, and pattern recognition, but they also redistribute epistemic authority and complicate responsibility when harm occurs. European regulation is developed in relation to market access, data governance, risk management, and product safety, yet remains fragmented regarding civil liability, organizational negligence, and the psychiatric standard of care. This Viewpoint examines how liability and standard of care should be understood when AI becomes part of psychiatric reasoning in Europe. It advances one central thesis: psychiatric AI requires justified integration supported by layered accountability within, but not determined by, European regulation. It presents a targeted doctrinal and normative synthesis of binding European Union instruments, regulatory guidance, selected national governance materials, and psychiatric, bioethical, legal, and digital mental health literature. It distinguishes binding law from guidance and policy, and separates ex ante regulation from ex post liability, and from professional standards of care. Four illustrative domains are analyzed: conversational or therapeutic chatbots, suicide prediction, digital phenotyping and passive monitoring, and large language model documentation. Psychiatric AI raises distinctive concerns because psychiatric judgment depends heavily on testimony, contextual meaning, therapeutic trust, risk interpretation, privacy, and liberty-sensitive decisions. Existing European instruments, including the AI Act, Medical Device Regulation, General Data Protection Regulation, revised Product Liability Directive, and European Health Data Space Regulation, establish governance duties, but do not provide a harmonized fault-based liability framework for AI-assisted health care. Regulatory compliance may inform later legal assessment, but it does not determine whether psychiatric care was reasonable. The proposed standard of justified integration requires knowledge of intended use and model limits, assessment of local and patient-level applicability, active clinical interpretation, disclosure when AI use is material to consent or trust, documentation in high-stakes decisions, and organizational audit. Accountability should be distributed across developers, deployers, and clinicians according to control and preventability. Mixed-fault scenarios are therefore likely to be common. The augmented-clinician model and layered accountability are offered as normative proposals rather than settled European legal standards. Clinicians should remain responsible for contextual, patient-centered judgment; developers for design, validation, documentation, and foreseeable misuse; and deployers for procurement, training, workflow integration, local validation, monitoring, and escalation. Future empirical research should evaluate effects on clinician reliance, documentation burden, patient outcomes, coercive interventions, therapeutic trust, and feasibility across differently resourced services.

documents.abstract: This review examines Lauren M. E. Goodlad's (2023) editor's introduction to Critical AI, "Humanities in the Loop," which argues for the constitutive participation of the interpretive humanities in artificial intelligence research, design, and governance. The review evaluates the essay's framing of three core dilemmas: reductive and contested meanings of "intelligence," problematic benchmarks for "AGI," and the intertwined issues of bias, error, and concentrated technological power. Goodlad's argument is situated within converging scholarly traditions, including the "stochastic parrots" critique advanced by Bender, post-Saussurean theory from Derrida, Bakhtin, and Jameson, and the historical critiques of Weizenbaum and Arendt regarding the separation of judgment from calculation. The review finds that the essay's central methodological contribution is its shift from langue to parole, language as system to language as enacted use, which reframes the human-machine relation around the irreducibility of vouloir-dire, the "desire to say," to statistical prediction. However, the review identifies three limitations: the essay's scope as an editor's introduction, its relative inattention to the political economy of AI development, and its predominantly English-language focus, which limits its applicability to low-resource language contexts where linguistic erasure, rather than anthropomorphic projection, is the primary risk. The review also considers counter-readings that position LLMs as "différance engines" actualizing deconstruction's insights. It concludes that Goodlad's most valuable contribution lies not in definitive answers but in carving out space for patient, theoretically informed critique that refuses both technodeterminist despair and techno-utopianism, positioning the humanities as essential interlocutors in the governance of accountable technology in the public interest.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, AI hallucinations have emerged as a significant challenge in human-AI interaction. Drawing on the perspective of algorithmic folk theories, this study combines textual analysis and in-depth interviews with both ordinary users and technical users to examine how they understand and respond to AI hallucinations. Users identify AI hallucinations by scrutinizing the AI’s reasoning process, making intuitive judgments, and conducting cross-validation, while their attitudes toward hallucinations vary. Users develop four types of algorithmic folk theories: the Human-AI Interaction Misalignment Theory, the Technical Limitations Theory, the Data Source Distortion Theory, and the Generative Rule Constraint Theory. They rise to four corresponding coping strategies: reducing communication errors, reconfiguring human-AI task allocation, intervening in data input while verifying outputs, and reducing AI’s processing load. This study further indicates how technological identity and sociotechnical contexts jointly shape algorithmic folk theories.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
